title: Four days after the flood
dek: When the Alder River broke its banks in Lowlands, a church kitchen became the town's dining room. A Rapid Response grant kept the stoves on.
author: Dana Okafor
quote: We didn't fill out a long form. Somebody called us, asked what we needed, and the money was there on Friday.
body:
The water came up overnight on March 11, 2024. By morning, 1,800 homes in Lowlands had water in them, and the town's two grocery stores were closed.

St. Brendan's had a kitchen, a parish hall and a list of volunteers. What it didn't have was money for food at that scale. The foundation's Rapid Response program sent $10,000 four days later, after one phone call and a one-page form.

One page, one call

Rapid Response grants are small on purpose. The point is speed: groups that are already helping shouldn't have to stop and write a proposal. The kitchen used the grant for food, gas for the stoves and a refrigerated trailer.

In five weeks, volunteers served 9,000 hot meals. When the kitchen closed, it handed its supplies and its volunteer list to the new Lowlands Flood Ready coalition, which now has a three-year Open Water grant to help the town prepare for the next one.

title: Bringing the marsh back to the river
dek: Farmers, the county and conservationists spent six years agreeing on a plan. Now 340 acres of Willow Marsh hold floodwater again.
author: Theo Lindqvist
quote: My grandfather drained this land. I'm the one letting the water back in, and I sleep better for it.
body:
Willow Marsh was drained for farming in the 1950s. Every big storm since then has sent the river straight into town.

Reconnecting the marsh meant moving a levee, buying easements from willing farmers and rebuilding drainage so the remaining fields stay dry. It took six years of meetings before the first excavator arrived.

Room for the river

The foundation funded the planning, the community meetings and the first season of planting. The county and state paid for construction. In the first winter, the marsh held back water that would have reached Main Street.

The work isn't finished. The next phase plants 40,000 native trees and shrubs along the new channel, much of it by students from Lowlands High School.

title: The bookmobile with a waiting list
dek: Libros Para Todos started with one van and a box of donated books. Now families wait for it at the end of every shift.
author: Marisol Vega
quote: My son asks for the van before he asks for the ice cream truck.
body:
Ferris Bend has no library and no bookstore. For many families, the nearest children's books are a 40-minute drive away.

Libros Para Todos parks its van outside the packing sheds at the end of each shift. Children choose a book to keep, and parents can sit in for a story time in Spanish, Mixteco or English.

Reading at home

The First Chapters grant pays for books, a part-time driver and training for parents who want to read aloud but never had books themselves. Teachers at Ferris Bend Elementary say they can tell which children visit the van.

title: A wage you can live on while you learn
dek: The Alder Building Trades Pathway pays people to train. Two years in, most graduates are working union jobs.
author: Dana Okafor
stat_label: of graduates hired within three months
quote: I couldn't afford to stop working to train. Here I didn't have to.
body:
Most apprenticeships expect you to already have tools, a car and a few months of savings. The Alder Building Trades Pathway assumes you don't.

Trainees earn $19 an hour from the first day. The program provides tools, work boots, a bus pass and childcare during class hours.

From training to a career

Four unions guarantee interviews to everyone who finishes. Of the first two cohorts, 83 percent were hired into registered apprenticeships within three months, and most are the first in their families to hold a union card.

title: Salmon are back in Kestrel Creek
dek: Tribal technicians removed two barriers and rebuilt a mile of stream. Last fall, coho spawned above the old culvert for the first time in sixty years.
author: Theo Lindqvist
quote: Our elders told us the fish would come back if we made room for them. They did.
body:
For sixty years, a road culvert on Kestrel Creek blocked fish from the best spawning gravel in the watershed.

The Kestrel Creek Tribe's natural resources department replaced it with a bridge, removed an old dam upstream and rebuilt a mile of stream channel with logs and boulders. Tribal youth did much of the survey and planting work as paid field technicians.

The first run

Last November, technicians counted 46 coho redds above the old culvert site. It is a small number, and a beginning. The grant now funds monitoring and the next mile of restoration.

title: Tenants who fixed their own buildings
dek: On Marlow's east side, tenants organized building by building, and won a repair fund that landlords pay into.
author: Marisol Vega
quote: For years we called the landlord one at a time. When we called together, things got fixed.
body:
Eastside Tenants United started with a single building and a shared spreadsheet of broken boilers, leaks and mold.

Tenants knocked on doors, held meetings in laundromats and documented every problem. When 14 buildings acted together, the owners agreed to a repair fund and a schedule.

What changed

The foundation's grant pays two organizers and a small emergency fund. Since 2024, tenants have tracked 312 urgent repairs through to completion, and four buildings have formed their own associations.
